title: Copy a door casing's profile with a contour gauge and set it to mark the cutting line on a board
instruction: Copy the casing's profile with the contour gauge, then stand the gauge on the plank across its pencilled cutting line, set to mark that cutting line, with the copied profile kept.
context: Fitting skirting board, flooring or a board end to an uneven door casing or wall (scribing) is a routine step for carpenters (SOC 47-2031, 670,090 US workers; BLS OEWS https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes472031.htm). The O*NET core tasks (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/47-2031.00) include "Measure and mark cutting lines on materials, using a ruler, pencil, chalk, and marking gauge." To measure and mark the cutting line for a board end, the carpenter copies the casing's profile with a contour gauge, then sets the gauge on the board at the line to mark it. One press captures the whole moulding at once and the gauge carries that outline to the board, but its fingers are held only by friction: it must be pressed level and lifted off without a finger moving, or the cut will not fit. The gauge is a USD 20 hardware-store tool (real_trial_cost_usd = 22); the casing and plank are job leftovers.
setup: A bench top carries three objects in one fixed starting layout (not randomised per seed), described from the far side of the bench to the side nearest the robot. A door-casing offcut lies loose and face up: colonial pattern, 57 mm wide, 17.5 mm thick, 200 mm long, pine, 85 g, friction 0.4 on the bench, its long axis pointing away from the robot. Across its width, from its inner edge, the moulded face has a raised bead 12 mm high and 10 mm wide, a 6 mm drop to a flat field 6 mm high and 18 mm wide, a cove rising to 12 mm over 12 mm, and a 5.5 mm step up to the 17.5 mm outer band, 17 mm wide. 150 mm nearer the robot a contour gauge stands upright on its finger tips, its long axis across the bench: a grey frame 254 x 22 x 10 mm holding 31 white plastic fingers at 8 mm pitch, each 76 mm long with a rounded 7 mm tip, each sliding up into the frame and held where it is left by friction; fully out, the tips sit 32 mm below the frame. All fingers start fully out; the gauge weighs 100 g. Nearest the robot a pine 1x6 plank (300 x 140 x 19 mm) is fixed to the bench, its long axis pointing away from the robot and its far end 50 mm nearer the robot than the gauge, with a pencilled cutting line drawn across it 30 mm from that end. The gauge's spine is clear for a grip anywhere along it; the casing slides if it is pushed.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 0 unless the copied profile matches the casing laid back against it at some offset and face (candidates are screened against every gate, then the lowest RMS is taken): at least 5 fingers at least 1 mm onto the casing within RMS 1.5 mm and worst 3.0 mm of its heights, the bench fingers within 30 mm of its edges within a peak-to-peak spread of 2.5 mm about one straight line, and that line (how level the frame was pressed) within 3 deg of level. Every feature of the casing's profile is at least 5.5 mm high and 10 mm wide, so these gates tell a copy from an unpressed gauge, a flat or tilted press, a flat block and a plain bevel of the same rise. Then 0.4; 1.0 if the gauge also stands upright (within 3 deg) on the plank across the cutting line: centre within 6 mm of the line and 10 mm of the plank's centre line, along the line within 5 deg, lowest finger tip within 3 mm of the plank top, and each hand's tool point more than 12 cm from the gauge centre in plan or more than 15 cm above the plank top. Capped at 0.5 if the casing's final position is more than 8 mm or its final heading more than 3 deg from where it lay. Possible: 0, 0.4, 0.5, 1.0.
fidelity: Rigid-body sim, 20 Hz. Each finger is a slide joint held by a 200 N/m drive re-latched each step, slipping past 0.5 N (estimate, as are finger mass 1.6 g, casing friction and the authored bead-and-cove profile, which is not a maker drawing). Fingers are 8 mm apart (real gauge about 1.5 mm), so 7-8 read the casing. The gauge ends standing on its outer fingers at the line, ready to trace: a scripted-demo constraint, not a traced board. Dream-1 run: 0.0; demo: 1.0
